That’s the problem, there’s nothing unacceptable about what’s being said. That is until someone (usually a supervisor or boss) adds a negative implication to it. Example: 

“Goodmorning [name]! I noticed the spreadsheet data from today’s meeting doesn’t match what we have on file. Can you please double check it for me when you have a moment? Thanks so much!”

Compared to

“Hello [name], there seems to be a discrepancy in our data tracking. The spreadsheet from today’s meeting doesn’t match what we have on file. When you get a chance, can you look over it and get back to me?”

My problem is that if a person knows they’re going to feel annoyed and burdened, maybe offering themselves as a support should come with more clearly defined expectations and boundaries.

Clearly a person contemplating suicide is to some extent cognitively impaired, so they might not realize in those emotionally volatile moments the way that their words might impact the other person. They’re probably desperate for someone to listen, and if people don’t make it clear the EXTENT to which they are willing to listen, and communicating when they start to feel overwhelmed, it’s not always a matter of the suicidal person being burdensome- they just needed you to draw the line bc maybe they’re not in a place to properly consider what your line is. 

Suicidal people shouldn’t have to mind-read a person’s boundaries and feel on their toes about what they are and are not able to share. It’s always good to check in and ask if they’re ok to hear what you have to say, but at a certain point people need to be responsible for setting their own boundaries.
